items.abstract: <jats:p>We construct a stationary ergodic process $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots$ such that each $X_{t}$ has the uniform distribution on the unit square and the length $L_{n}$ of the shortest path through the points $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ is not asymptotic to a constant times the square root of $n$. In other words, we show that the Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley [Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 55 (1959) 299–327] theorem does not extend from the case of independent uniformly distributed random variables to the case of stationary ergodic sequences with uniform marginal distributions.</jats:p>
title: Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley theorem for stationary ergodic sequences: A counterexample

items.abstract: <jats:p>Stationary drift vortices in plasmas are studied analytically. It is demonstrated how to obtain explicit monopole vortex solutions of this kind. They contain a core region with closed streamlines, and have an arbitrary radial profile. A simple expression giving the propagation velocity of the vortices is obtained, and it is found that for the vortices to be stationary, the velocity should not be close to the phase velocity of linear waves. This requires a large amplitude.</jats:p>
title: Stationary drift vortices with large amplitude

items.abstract: <jats:p>Concept drift represents a fundamental challenge in intrusion detection systems, as the non-stationary nature of network environments causes continuous shifts in data distributions that progressively compromise model performance. Existing approaches typically detect concept drift through distribution-based statistics and react using fixed model update mechanisms, without explicitly leveraging the structural evolution of the data stream to guide adaptive model expansion. In this work, we propose a drift-aware adaptive framework where the structural evolution of data streams on the Grassmann manifold guides the controlled expansion of a dynamic Mixture-of-Experts architecture. Incoming data windows are represented as subspaces whose temporal evolution is modeled using Grassmannian geometry. Drift is quantified through distances between consecutive subspaces, providing a principled measure of geometric change in the latent feature space. Rather than relying on uniform adaptation strategies, the proposed framework leverages the magnitude of detected drift to guide selective model expansion. When significant geometric deviations are identified, new experts based on Hoeffding Tree classifiers are instantiated to capture emerging subspace structures, while previously learned experts are retained to preserve historical knowledge, mitigate catastrophic forgetting, and maintain a balance between stability and plasticity under non-stationary conditions. Experimental results on the NSL-KDD, CIDDS-001, and IoTID20 intrusion detection benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach enhances classification performance under concept drift, achieving recall rates above 98.63%, false alarm rates below 5.45%, and throughput of up to 9551.72 instances per second, supporting near real-time intrusion detection.</jats:p>
title: Grassmannian-guided adaptive mixture-of-experts for concept drift in non-stationary environments
